sentences.text: Thecodontosaurus was a small, two-legged creature measuring about two meters in total length.
Its scientific name translates to "socket-tooth," referring to how its teeth sat in individual holes rather than being fused to the jawbone.
The animal possessed numerous small to medium-sized teeth that were serrated and shaped like leaves.
On average, this species stood thirty centimeters tall, weighed eleven kilograms, and measured one point two meters long.
It had a narrow skull equipped with curved teeth designed for processing plant material.
Modern reconstructions indicate its neck was proportionally shorter than that of more advanced ancient sauropodomorphs.
The largest known individuals of this species reached an estimated length of two point five meters.
Analysis of muscle attachments reveals it was capable of running at high speeds on its hind legs.
Despite its speed, it used its weaker front limbs to grasp, cut, and carry vegetation to its mouth.
Excavations began in the autumn of 1834 when surgeon Henry Riley and curator Samuel Stutchbury dug at the Durdham Down quarry in Clifton.
They published an initial description in 1836, creating a new genus name without assigning a specific species at that time.
The genus Thecodontosaurus was officially named in 1836 by Henry Riley and Samuel Stutchbury.
John Morris later provided the complete species name Thecodontosaurus antiquus in 1843.
Originally, Riley and Stutchbury classified the animal as a member of Squamata, the group containing lizards and snakes.
There are fourteen recorded fossil occurrences of Thecodontosaurus listed in the Paleobiology Database.
Studies of muscle attachment suggest the animal was an extremely fast bipedal runner.
It utilized its weaker front limbs to grasp, cut, and carry vegetation to its mouth.
Its front limbs were not strong enough for heavy lifting but served to process plant food.
Thomas Huxley was the first to recognize Thecodontosaurus as a dinosaur in 1870, though he incorrectly placed it in the Scelidosauridae.
When Richard Owen coined the term Dinosauria in 1842, he did not recognize Thecodontosaurus as a dinosaur.
Later, the animal was placed in Anchisauridae or its own family Thecodontosauridae alongside Agrosaurus.
The parent group of the genus Thecodontosaurus is Sauropodomorpha.
Thecodontosaurus is considered the best-known and most primitive representative of sauropodomorph dinosaurs.
Currently, the only valid species is T. antiquus.
In 2007, some remains were separated into the distinct genus Pantydraco caducus.
In 2020, Ballell, Rayfield, and Benton suggested that Pantydraco caducus might be a taxon of uncertain validity or a juvenile of Thecodontosaurus antiquus.
Remains of Thecodontosaurus are primarily found in Triassic fissure fillings in southern England.
Thecodontosaurus lived between 206 and 201 million years ago during the Rhaetian age in what is now Europe.
While once thought to date to the late Carnian, recent studies indicate these deposits date to the Rhaetian.
In 2000, Michael Benton suggested that a robust morph found in the population might represent either a second species or sexual dimorphism.
Its small size has been explained as a case of insular dwarfism.
The hypothesis that carnivorous prosauropods with the body of Thecodontosaurus and slicing teeth existed has been totally discredited.
Although defended by Michael Cooper in 1981, the hypothesis that such creatures existed has now been totally discredited.
In 2000, Michael Benton noted a robust morph in the population, viewing it as either a possible second species or more likely a case of sexual dimorphism.
